<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|work|6975|work}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''To work at arm’s length.''' See ''arm’s-length.''—'''To work at case.''' See ''case''<sup>2</sup>.—'''To work double tides.''' See ''tide''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To work free.''' See ''free.''—'''To work off,''' to be evacuated or eliminated, as poison from the system, by the bowels or kidneys.—'''To work on''' or '''upon.''' (''a'') To act or operate upon; exert a force or active influence upon; affect.
{{smaller block|A mark, and a hope, and a subject for every sophister in religion to ''work on.'' {{right|''Donne'', Letters, xc.}}}}
{{smaller block|We were now at a great loss, not knowing what course to take, for we tempted him [an Indian] with Beads, Money, Hatchets, Macheats, or long Knives; but nothing would ''work on'' him. {{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 13.}}}}
(''b''†) To rely on.
{{smaller block|<poem>“I schal, sire,” seide the child, “for saufliche y hope
I may ''worche on'' ȝour word to wite him fro harm.”</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 257.}}}}
'''To work with,''' to endeavor to influence, as with reasoning, entreaty, etc.; strive with in order to influence in some particular way; labor with.
{{smaller block|<poem>I ''wrought with'' him in private, to divert him
From your assur’d destruction, had he met you.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Little French Lawyer, iii. 1.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Act, Work'', etc. See ''act.''

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To prepare by labor; manipulate: as, to ''work'' soil or clay.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ffate lande ydounged moist and wel ''ywrought''
Onyons desire.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 82.}}}}
{{smaller block|When special pains are taken to “''work'' the butter” thoroughly, thus more effectually getting rid of the water and buttermilk, it keeps for a much longer period in a “sweet” condition. {{right|''Science'', XVI. 71.}}}}
'''2.''' To convert to use by labor or effort; operate: as, to ''work'' a quarry; to ''work'' a scheme.
{{smaller block|The head member of the company that ''worked'' the mines was Mr. Peter Garstin, and the same company received the rent for the Sugar Loaf. {{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xi.}}}}
{{smaller block|As the claim was ''worked'' back, the long tom was extended by means of sluice boxes, until a dozen or more miners were shoveling dirt into them on both sides.
{{right|''The Century'', XLII. 140.}}}}
'''3.''' To make; form; fashion; execute; mold.
{{smaller block|<poem>Allas! that we wer ''wroughte''
In worlde women to be.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 153.}}}}
{{smaller block|A mong other, a wonderfull gretnesse that be rygtht Curiusely ''wrogth'' and arn fyne gold garnyshed over all with stones of gret Pryse.
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|That was one of the famous cups of Tours, ''wrought'' by Martin Dominique.
{{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Here is a sword I have ''wrought'' thee.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Sigurd, ii.}}}}
'''4.''' To decorate or ornament, as with needlework; embroider.
{{smaller block|<poem>She hath a clout of mine,
''Wrought'' with good Coventry.</poem>
{{right|''Phillada flouts me'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 311).}}}}
{{smaller block|You shall see my ''wrought'' shirt hang out at my breeches; you shall know me.
{{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, I., v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Ay, I have lost my thimble and a skein of Coventry blue I had to ''work'' Gregory Litchfield a handkerchief.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Gipsies Metamorphosed.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A shape with amice wrapp’d around,
With a ''wrought'' Spanish baldric bound,
Like pilgrim from beyond the sea.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., vi. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A damask napkin ''wrought'' with horse and hound.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Audley Court.}}}}

'''5.''' To do, perform, or accomplish; bring about; effect; produce; cause: as, to ''work'' mischief; to ''work'' a change; to ''work'' wonders.
{{smaller block|<poem>A felle man in fight, fuerse on his enimys,
And in batell full bigge, & myche bale ''wroght.''</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3971.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Allas! wrecchis, what haue we ''wrought?''
To byggly blys we bothe wer brought.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 30.}}}}
{{smaller block|Than he taught hir ther a pley that she ''wrought'' after many tymes, ffor he taught hir to do come a grete river ouer all theras her liked. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 312.}}}}
{{smaller block|For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, ''worketh'' for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. {{right|2 Cor. iv. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|Changes were ''wrought'' in the parts.
{{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, i., Expl.}}}}
{{smaller block|Not long after there fell out an unexpected Accident, that suddenly ''wrought'' the Lords Confusion.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 110.}}}}
{{smaller block|The emancipation is observed, in the islands, to have ''wrought'' for the negro a benefit as sudden as when a thermometer is brought out of the shade into the sun.
{{right|''Emerson'', West Indian Emancipation.}}}}

'''6.''' To put or set in motion or action: as, to ''work'' one’s fingers.
{{smaller block|<poem>The mariners all ’gan ''work'' the ropes,
Where they were wont to do.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', Ancient Mariner, v.}}}}
{{smaller block|They are every one of them dead dolls, wooden, ''worked'' with wires. {{right|''Kingsley'', Hypatia, xiii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nodding in a familiar manner to the coachman, as if any one of them would be quite equal to getting on the box and ''working'' the team down street as well as he.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, i. 5.}}}}

'''7.''' (''a'') To direct the action or movements of; manage; handle: as, to ''work'' a sawmill. {{smaller block|Mere personal valour could not supply want of knowledge in building and ''working'' ships. {{right|''Arbuthnot.''}}}}
(''b'') In ''music'', to handle or treat (a voice-part or a theme).—'''8.''' To bring by action or motion into some particular state, usually indicated by an adverb or adverbial adjunct, as ''in'', ''out'', ''over'', ''up'', etc. See phrases below.
{{smaller block|Practise all things chiefly at two several times, the one when the mind is best disposed, the other when it is worst disposed; that by the one you may gain a great step, by the other you may ''work out'' the knots and stonds of the mind. {{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii. 296.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>So the pure limpid stream, when foul with stains
Of rushing torrents and descending rains,
''Works'' itself clear, and as it runs refines.</poem>{{right|''Addison'', Cato, i. 6.}}}}
'''9.''' To manage or turn to some particular course or way of thinking or acting by insidious means; influence in some respect by plying with arguments, urgings, threats, bribes, etc.; prevail on or gain over; induce; persuade; lead: as, to ''work'' the committee; to ''work'' the jury.
{{smaller block|There is noe hope that they will ever be ''wrought'' to serve faythfully agaynst theyr old frendes and kinsemen. {{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I will try his temper;
And, if I find him apt for my employments,
I’ll ''work'' him to my ends.</poem>{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Clergy being thus brought on, on the nine and twentieth of April, the Cardinal came into the House of Commons, to ''work'' them also. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 270.}}}}
{{smaller block|Many of the Jews were ''wrought'' into the belief that Herod was the Messias. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., i. 3.}}}} '''10.''' To excite by degrees; bring into a state of perturbation or passion; provoke; agitate.
{{smaller block|<poem>Some passion
That ''works'' him strongly.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1. 144.}}}}
{{smaller block|Sir Lucius has ''wrought'' me to it. He has left me full of rage—and I’ll fight this evening, that so much good passion mayn’t be wasted. {{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, iv. 1.}}}}
'''11.''' To succeed in effecting, attaining, or making; win by labor; achieve: as, to ''work'' a passage through something.
{{smaller block|Through winds and waves and storms he ''works'' his way.
{{right|''Addison'', Cato, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Some months afterwards Amory made his appearance at Calcutta, having ''worked'' his way out before the mast from the Cape. {{right|''Thackeray'', Pendennis, xxv.}}}}
{{smaller block|We passed heavily laden junks slowly ''working'' their way upstream amidst what to any but the Chinese would have appeared insurmountable difficulties.
{{right|''The Century'', XLI. 729.}}}}
'''12.''' To endeavor; attempt; try.
{{smaller block|By reason she was fast in the latch of our cable . . . she could not cleare her selfe as she ''wrought'' to doe.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 43.}}}}
'''13.''' To operate on, as a purgative or other drug; purge.
{{smaller block|Every time it operates, it carries off a Distemper; but if your Blood ’s Wholesome, and your Body Sound, it will ''work'' you no more than the same quantity of Ginger bread.
{{right|Quoted in ''Ashton’s'' Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne,}}
{{right|[II. 106.}}}}
'''14.''' To ply one’s trade, calling, vocation, or business in; carry on operations in or on: as, to ''work'' a district in canvassing for a publication. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|I’ve ''worked'' both town and country on gold fish. I’ve served both Brighton and Hastings.
{{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, II. 91.}}}}
{{smaller block|As a general rule, the “casual ward” of a workhouse, so far from being the temporary refuge of deserving poor, is a place of rendezvous for thieves and prostitutes and other vagabonds of the lowest class, gangs of whom ''work'' allotted districts, and make their circuits with as much regularity as the Judges.
{{right|''A. Doyle'', quoted in Ribton-Turner’s Vagrants and [Vagrancy, p. 293.}}}}
{{smaller block|The first day I started alone to explore the forest with gun and dog, leaving my friends to ''work'' the river.
{{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XLIII. 632.}}}}
'''15.''' To exact labor or service from; keep busy or employed: as, he ''works'' his horses too hard.
{{smaller block|Until the year 1820, the people [in Great Britain] had been forbidden to combine. Their only power against employers who ''worked'' them as many hours a day as they dared, and paid them wages as small as they could, who took their children and locked them up in unwholesome factories, was in combination, and they were forbidden to combine.
{{right|''W. Besant'', Fifty Years Ago, p. 80.}}}}
'''16.''' To solve: as, to ''work'' a sum in arithmetic or a problem in algebra. [Colloq.]—'''17.''' To cause to ferment: said of anything which is put into a liquid for that purpose.—'''To work an observation.''' {{smaller|See ''observation.''—'''To work a traverse.''' See ''traverse sailing'', under ''sailing.''—'''To work in.''' (''a'') To intermix, as one material with another, in the process of manufacture or the like; weave or stir in: as, he ''worked'' the good yarn ''in'' with the bad. (''b'') To cause to enter or penetrate by repeated efforts: as, the wire was slowly ''worked in.''—'''To work into.''' (''a'') To introduce artfully; insinuate: as, he easily ''works'' himself ''into'' confidence by}} his plausibility. (''b'') To change or alter by gradual process or influence.
{{smaller block|<poem>This imperious man will ''work'' us all
From princes ''into'' pages.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., ii. 2. 47.}}}}
'''To work off''', to get rid of; free or be freed from, or from the effects of; discharge; evacuate: as, to ''work off'' the effects of a debauch.—'''To work one’s passage''', to give one’s work or services as an equivalent for passage-money.—'''To work one’s will.''' See ''will''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To work out.''' (''a'') To effect or procure by continued labor or exertion; accomplish.
{{smaller block|''Work out'' your own salvation with fear and trembling.
{{right|Phil. ii. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Who can hide,
When the malicious Fates are bent
On ''working out'' an ill intent?</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', The Waggoner, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O lift your natures up:
Embrace our aims: ''work out'' your freedom.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, ii.}}}}
(''b'') To elaborate; develop; reduce to order; study out.
{{smaller block|She [Italy] did not ''work out'' the basilican type for herself; she left it to others to do that for her, and consequently never perfectly understood what she undertook or why it was done.
{{right|''J. Fergusson'', Hist. Arch., I. 428.}}}}
{{smaller block|The minerals, which are now in the British Museum, were ''worked out'' by Mr. Davies of that establishment.
{{right|''Amer. Jour. Sci.'', 3d ser., XLI. 406.}}}}
(''c'') To solve, as a problem.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Mal.'' M,—Malvolio; M,—why, that begins my name—
''Fab.'' Did not I say he would ''work'' it ''out?''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 5. 139.}}}}
(''d'') To erase; efface; remove.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tears of joy, for your returning spilt,
''Work out'' and expiate our former guilt.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Astræa Redux, l. 275.}}}} (''e'') To exhaust: as, to ''work out'' a mine or quarry.—'''To work out a day’s work''' (''naut.''), to compute a ship’s position from the course and distance sailed.—'''To work the twig.''' See ''twig''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To work up.''' (''a'') To excite; stir up; raise; rouse.

{{smaller block|It is no very hard Matter to ''work up'' a heated and devout Imagination to the Fancy of Raptures and Ecstasies and Mystical Unions. {{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, III. iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|We cannot but tremble to consider what we are capable of being ''wrought up'' to, against all the ties of nature, love, honour, reason, and religion. {{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 172.}}}}
{{smaller block|They [the Moslems] ''work'' themselves ''up'' to such agonies of rage and lamentation that some, it is said, have given up the ghost from the mere effect of mental excitement. {{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Clive.}}}}

(''b'') To use up in the process of manufacture or the like; expend in any work: as, we have ''worked up'' all our materials.

{{smaller block|The industry of the people ''works up'' all their native commodities to the last degree of manufacture. {{right|''Swift.''}}}}

(''c'') To expand; enlarge; elaborate: as, to ''work up'' a story or an article from a few hints.

{{smaller block|We have read of “Handkerchief Moody,” who for some years persisted in always appearing among men with his face covered with a handkerchief—an incident which Hawthorne has ''worked up'' in his weird manner into the story of “The Minister with the Black Veil.” {{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 454.}}}}

(''d'') To master by careful study or research: as, to ''work up'' a theme. (''e'') To achieve or attain by special effort: as, to ''work up'' a reputation for one’s self. (''f'') ''Naut.'', to discipline or punish by setting at an unnecessary or hateful job, like scraping the anchor-chain. Such a piece of work is called a ''working-up job.''—'''To work water.''' See the quotation.

{{smaller block|Water is also frequently carried over from the boiler with the steam. When this occurs the boiler is said to prime, or to ''work water.'' {{right|''Forney'', Locomotive, p. 170.}}}}

'''work''' (wėrk), ''n.''   [< ME. ''work'', ''werk'', ''wurc'', ''worc'', ''werc'', ''weorc'', < AS. ''weorc'', ''worc'', ''werc'' = OS. OFries. D. ''werk'' = LG. ''wark'' = OHG. ''werch'', ''werah'', MHG. ''werc'', G. ''werk'' = Icel. Sw. ''verk'' = Dan. ''værk'' = Goth. ''ga-waurki''; cf. Gr. ἔργον, work: see ''work'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' Effort or exertion directed to the accomplishment of some purpose or end; expenditure of strength, energy, etc.; toil; labor; striving.
{{smaller block|Fie upon this quiet life! I want ''work''.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 118.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Man hath his daily ''work'' of body or mind
Appointed.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 618.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Here, ''work'' enough to watch
The Master work, and catch
Hints of the proper craft.</poem>{{right|''Browning'', Rabbi Ben Ezra.}}}}
'''2.''' Opportunity of expending labor (physical or mental) in some useful or remunerative way, especially as a means of earning a livelihood; employment; something to do: as, to be out of ''work''; to look for ''work''.—'''3.''' That upon which one is employed or engaged, and in the accomplishment of which labor is expended or some operation performed; a task, undertaking, enterprise, or project.
{{smaller block|If it would please Him whose ''worke'' it is to direct me to speake such a word over the sea as the good old woman of Abel did over the wall in the like exigent.
{{right|''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 33.}}}}
{{smaller block|The great ''work'' of erecting a way of worshipping of Christ in church fellowship.
{{right|''N. Morton'', New England’s Memorial, p. 160.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
